headline: Stale sessions are deleted and password checks run one at a time
summary: The server now deletes stale sessions every hour and no longer stores one for health checks or API clients. Password checks run one at a time with up to eight waiting, request fields that a visitor can store are held to fixed limits, and a vault-key rotation keeps every file it does not rewrite. Share links and tokens no longer appear in the server's logs. A signed-in page left open now shows the session-expired prompt once the idle timeout passes, and an idle timeout longer than 30 minutes now takes effect.

items.title: Vendored blamejs moves to 0.20.38
items.body:
Four changes in the framework affect this server. The CADF audit export writes `blamejs:unattributed` as the initiator ID of an entry with no actor and `blamejs:unidentified` as the target ID of an entry with no target, where it wrote `unknown` and `n/a`, and it no longer types an entry with no actor as a user account. CSV exports write a cell that opens with `|` unchanged, and a cell that opens with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, a tab or a line break is still prefixed with an apostrophe. The client and browser certificate authorities each keep their own CRL number, in `ca.crl-number` and `ca-browser.crl-number`.

A password check against a stored Argon2id hash with a memory cost above 524288 KiB, a time cost above 24 or a parallelism above 16 now fails without running Argon2id. The hashes the server writes use m=65536, t=3, p=4.

items.title: Purge stale sessions, and stop storing one for health checks and API clients
items.body:
Every request that arrived without a session cookie stored a new session of about 9 KB, and the server deleted a session only when a request presented it after it had expired. The session database lives in `/dev/shm` by default, which is held in memory. The Docker health check requests `/health` every 30 seconds, which stored 2,880 sessions and about 25 MB a day. The probes in `deploy/kubernetes.yml` stored 11,520 sessions and about 100 MB a day. Each request from the desktop sync client stored one as well.

The server now deletes stale sessions once at startup and then every hour. A session is stale when it has been idle for longer than `SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT`, when it is past its seven-day lifetime, or when it is older than `SESSION_ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT_MS`. The server already refused to accept any of those sessions. When the deletions leave the session database file at least half empty and at least 16 MiB in size, the server rewrites the file, which shrinks it to the size of the sessions that remain.

A request without a session cookie no longer stores a session when it carries an `Authorization: Bearer` credential, when it is a `HEAD` or `OPTIONS` request, or when it is a `GET` of `/health`, `/sitemap.xml`, `/manifest.json` or `/.well-known/blamejs-pubkey`. The server sends no `Set-Cookie` header in the response to such a request.

items.title: Apply the configured session timeouts when a session is saved
items.body:
After each request the server saved the session data through a call that applied the framework's default timeouts instead of the configured ones: 30 minutes idle, and 12 hours from creation. An idle timeout longer than 30 minutes therefore had no effect beyond 30 minutes, whether it was set with `SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT` or in the admin settings: a session idle for longer than 30 minutes ended after its next request. A `SESSION_ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT_MS` longer than 12 hours had no effect either. The same call also reset the idle timer on every request. A signed-in page sends a session check every minute, so a page left open never reached the idle timeout.

Saving a session now applies the configured timeouts and leaves the idle timer alone. A signed-in page left idle for the idle timeout now shows the "Session expired" prompt. `SESSION_ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT_MS` now defaults to `43200000`. That is 12 hours, the limit sessions already had in practice. Set it to `0` to remove the limit.

items.title: Carry every file a vault-key rotation does not rewrite
items.body:
`scripts/vault-key-rotate.js` builds a rotated copy of the data directory and then swaps it into place. It copied a fixed list of files into that copy, and everything else stayed behind in the retained `data.old.<timestamp>/` directory: the revocation lists and generation watermarks of both certificate authorities, the audit signing key, uploaded logos, audit archives, the markers that record one-time migrations, and certificates kept as symbolic links. Releases up to and including 1.15.7 are affected.

The rotation now copies everything under the data directory into the rotated copy except the files it rewrites and transient files. It rewrites the encrypted database, the sealed database key, the vault key and the other re-sealed keys. The transient files are locks, temporary files and a plaintext working database. It recreates each symbolic link with its original target.

If you rotated the vault key with an earlier release and still have the `data.old.<timestamp>/` directory it left, the files listed above are in that directory.

items.title: Answer an unusable sign-in email address like a wrong password
items.body: A sign-in attempt with an email address longer than 254 characters wrote the whole address to the audit log, and an address containing a line break failed with HTTP 500. Both now get the same 401 response as a wrong password, after the same password check, and the audit entry records the length of the address instead of the address.

items.title: Encode an apostrophe in a download's file name
items.body: The `filename*` parameter of a download's `Content-Disposition` header left an apostrophe unencoded, which RFC 8187 does not allow. The framework now builds the header: `filename` holds an ASCII form of the name, `filename*` holds the full name percent-encoded, and a name containing a carriage return, line feed or NUL is sent as `download`.

items.title: Remove C1 control characters from file names
items.body: Renaming a file and naming a vault file removed C0 control characters and DEL but kept the C1 range, U+0080 to U+009F, and a Tailscale display name kept it as well. Those characters are now removed.

items.title: Keep the Vary tokens that other layers set
items.body: A response marked `Cache-Control: no-store` had its `Vary` header replaced with `Cookie`, which dropped a `Vary: Origin` set for CORS. `Cookie` is now added to the existing header.

items.title: Migrate files larger than 64 MiB from local disk to S3
items.body: The local-to-S3 storage migration read each file with a 64 MiB limit, so every larger file was reported as failed and stayed on local disk. The migration now reads each file as a stream, without blocking the server while it reads, and migrates files up to 2 GiB. The upload to S3 holds one file in memory at a time, and a file larger than 2 GiB is reported as failed and stays on local disk.

items.title: Stop reporting a damaged sealed vault key as a wrong passphrase
items.body: When the server could not read the header of `vault.key.sealed`, the Disable action for vault key passphrase wrapping on the admin Security tab returned HTTP 401 with "passphrase rejected", the response for a wrong passphrase. It now returns HTTP 500, and the server logs an error whose message starts with "unseal failed:". `scripts/vault-passphrase-remove.js` and `scripts/vault-passphrase-rotate.js` print the header error without the line that asks you to check the passphrase. A wrong passphrase gets the same responses as before. The Enable and Disable actions now refuse a passphrase longer than 4,096 bytes with HTTP 400.

items.title: Load the audit signing key again after a failed load
items.body:
The server loads the audit signing key the first time an audit operation needs it: archiving, retention cleanup, a chain checkpoint, or a chain or archive verification. When that load failed, the server did not try it again, and each of those operations failed with the same error until a restart. The server now tries the load again the next time an operation needs the key.

With `AUDIT_SIGNING_MODE=wrapped`, the server loads the key again only when it can read the passphrase without a prompt: from the file named by `BLAMEJS_AUDIT_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE_FILE`, or from `BLAMEJS_AUDIT_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE` while that variable is still set. The framework removes the variable when it first reads it. When a load fails after that, each later operation returns the same error until the server restarts.

items.title: Remove an audit archive bundle whose check stopped with an error
items.body: The server writes each audit archive bundle, reads it back and checks it before it deletes the archived entries from the live audit log. It removed a bundle that failed the check. It left a bundle whose check stopped with an error, such as a failed decryption, in the archive directory, and the bundle's entries stayed in the live log. The next archive run then wrote the same entries into a second bundle. The server now removes the bundle in both cases.

items.title: Answer a request with an error when the session store fails
items.body: When the server could not read or create a session, it continued the request without one, and a signed-in visitor appeared signed out. It now answers the request with HTTP 500 and logs the failure as `Unhandled server error`.

items.title: Restore the error text for a chunk the server could not save
items.body: When the server could not save an uploaded chunk, its error response read "Invalid nodePath." The response now reads "Invalid path." in that case.

items.title: Name `BACKUP_PASSPHRASE_HASH` when the server cannot check it
items.body: When `BACKUP_PASSPHRASE_HASH` was not an Argon2id hash, the server refused every passphrase as wrong: a backup run returned "Incorrect backup passphrase." and a restore returned "Invalid passphrase." With blamejs 0.20.38, an Argon2id hash with a memory cost above 524288 KiB, a time cost above 24 or a parallelism above 16 would fail the same way. A backup run or restore with either kind of value now fails with HTTP 500 and a message that names `BACKUP_PASSPHRASE_HASH`, and the server logs the same message.

items.title: Limit concurrent password checks
items.body:
Each Argon2id password check uses 64 MiB of memory. The server ran up to eight checks at once, 512 MiB in all, and queued every further check with no limit, so a burst of sign-in or share-link unlock attempts kept that memory in use until the queue drained.

One check now runs at a time and up to eight more wait. A check that arrives while the queue is full is refused with HTTP 503 and `Retry-After: 2`, and no Argon2id work starts for it. The limit covers sign-in, registration and invitation acceptance, password reset, password and email changes on the profile page, the setup wizard, share-link and stash passwords, and backup passphrase checks. A refused check does not count as a failed attempt for account lockout or for the share-link and stash unlock backoff, and a password reset link stays usable after a refused submit. The public upload page waits for the `Retry-After` delay and retries a refused upload start up to `UPLOAD_RETRIES` times.

Sealing or unsealing the vault key from the admin Security tab, loading a wrapped audit signing key, and encrypting or checking an audit archive also run Argon2id. The server now runs them one at a time together with the password checks. They wait for a free slot and are not refused. A backup or restore runs its Argon2id work in a worker thread, and this limit does not apply to it.

items.title: Stop putting the skipped-file count into notification emails as HTML
items.body: `/drop/init` and `/stash/:slug/init` stored the `skippedCount` they were sent without checking it, and the upload emails inserted that value into their HTML without escaping it. An anonymous uploader could put links and other HTML into the admin notification email, and, when the upload listed skipped files, into the confirmation sent to the address the uploader supplied. The init routes now refuse a `skippedCount` that is not a whole number, and the emails write the stored value as a number.

items.title: Refuse an invalid address in a bundle's allowed-email list
items.body: `/drop/init` dropped each address in `allowedEmails` that failed validation and kept the rest. When every address failed, the bundle was created without the email restriction. An invalid address is now refused with HTTP 400, and the list holds at most 100 addresses.

items.title: Hold stored request fields to fixed limits
items.body:
`/drop/init` and `/stash/:slug/init` refuse a `fileCount` or `skippedCount` that is not a whole number and a `skippedFiles` value that is not a list. They keep the first 50 skipped entries, with each path cut to 500 characters and each reason to 100. The server previously stored these values at any size.

A sync rename to a path longer than 500 characters is refused with HTTP 400, which is the limit uploads already applied. Vault uploads refuse an encapsulated key that is not 1,568 bytes, an IV that is not 24 bytes, and a batch ID that is not 1 to 64 letters, digits, hyphens or underscores, and a vault public key, seed or re-encrypted key must be sent as canonical base64. A vault upload's MIME type that is longer than 255 bytes or contains a line break is stored as `application/octet-stream`. Passkey registration stores at most 8 distinct transport hints. An audit entry stores at most 4,096 characters of details, 320 characters of an email address and 128 characters of an ID, and the entry for an uploaded file records the file name as the file record stores it.

items.title: Refuse a symbolic link during a local-to-S3 storage migration
items.body: The local-to-S3 storage migration read each stored file with a call that follows symbolic links, so a link planted at an upload path made the migration copy the file it pointed to into the bucket. The migration now reads through the same function as downloads, which opens the file with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and a link fails that file's migration with "storage object not found".

items.title: Move the base image to a build with a fixed zlib
items.body: The v1.15.7 image ships zlib 1.3.2-r5, which Trivy reports as affected by CVE-2026-85091 (MEDIUM, a heap buffer overflow). The base image is now the `cgr.dev/chainguard/wolfi-base` build of 2026-10-02, which ships zlib 1.3.2.1_rc20260601-r0, the version Wolfi lists as fixed.

items.title: Keep share links and tokens out of the server's logs
items.body:
When a request failed, the server wrote its request path to stdout or stderr. The path of a share link holds the bundle or file share ID, and a password-reset, email-verification or invite link holds its token. Anyone who could read the container output or a log aggregator could therefore open those bundles and files or use those links. The router's `route error` and `middleware error` lines wrote the path with its query string, and the server's `Unhandled server error`, `requireAdmin denied` and `security pipeline error` lines wrote it as well. The `Bundle unlock lockout`, `Zip skip`, `[files/download] Error` and `[migration] Failed to migrate file` lines named a share ID, and storage errors named the storage key, which holds both share IDs of a file.

The server now answers every failed request through its own error handler, and the router writes no line for it. A server error is logged as `Unhandled server error`, and a request refused with a 4xx status is logged at debug level as `Request refused`, with its status, code and route pattern. A refusal with HTTP 401, 403 or 429 is also recorded in the audit log, as before. The path in the server's lines is the route pattern, such as `/b/:shareId/download`, without the query string. A request that fails before a route matches is shown with each path segment of 32 or more letters, digits, `-` or `_` replaced by `:token`. Each 64-character hexadecimal value in a log message or a text field, such as an error message or a storage path, is written as `[redacted]`, and so is the value of a field whose name contains `share`. A field whose name ends in `Id`, such as `bundleId` or `userId`, is written unchanged. The `Unhandled server error` line now carries the request ID that the audit log records for the request.

Audit events forwarded to a SIEM carry the route pattern in `path`, and each 64-character hexadecimal value in `details` is replaced by `[redacted]`. A new `pathDigest` field holds the first 32 hexadecimal characters of the SHA3-512 hash of the full path. Two events for the same share link carry the same `pathDigest`. The audit log that the server stores keeps the full request path, so an administrator can search it for a share link, and an audit export carries the full path as well. In the stored log, the `details` of an entry for a refused request (HTTP 401, 403 or 429) and of a refused admin request now give the route pattern, and a password-reset token in the path is no longer copied into them.

Log output written by earlier releases still contains share IDs and tokens, and a share link in it stays usable until its bundle is deleted or expires. Delete that output, or restrict who can read it. A reverse proxy's access log also records the full request line of every share link. The nginx and Apache examples in `deploy/reverse-proxy/` and the ingress example in `deploy/kubernetes.yml` use the proxy's default access log. The Caddyfile example writes no access log unless a `log` directive is added.

items.title: Return a share link on a repeated finalize only to the bundle's owner or uploader
items.body: A repeated `POST /drop/finalize/:bundleId` or `POST /stash/:slug/finalize/:bundleId` for a complete bundle without an owner, such as a signed-out upload or a stash upload, returned the bundle's share link to any caller that had the bundle ID. A bundle ID appears in audit events, in sync connection log lines and in the request lines a reverse proxy logs. A repeated finalize of such a bundle now returns the link only to a caller that sends the bundle's finalize token. Any other caller gets the HTTP 404 reply an unknown bundle gets. A bundle with an owner returns the link only to its owner, as before. A bundle finalized by an earlier release has no finalize token on record, so a repeated finalize for it succeeds only for its owner.

items.title: Apply an API key's stash, bundle and certificate binding on the drop routes
items.body: A sync API key carries the user ID of the admin who issued it, and it can be bound to a stash, to one bundle or to a client certificate. `POST /drop/init`, `POST /drop/file/:bundleId`, `POST /drop/chunk/:bundleId` and `POST /drop/finalize/:bundleId` checked only that user ID. A stash client's key could therefore start bundles in the issuing admin's account, upload into the admin's own sync bundles and replace files there, and receive the share link of the admin's completed bundles. A key bound to a certificate also worked on these routes without its certificate. These routes now apply the binding checks the other bundle routes apply. A key bound to a stash reaches only that stash's bundles, a key bound to a bundle reaches only that bundle, and a key bound to a certificate works only with that certificate. A key bound to a stash or a bundle gets HTTP 403 on `POST /drop/init`.

items.title: Refuse sync bundles that have no owner
items.body: `POST /drop/init` accepted `bundleType: "sync"` from a caller that was not signed in. The bundle it created was complete from the start and accepted files, including replacements of existing files, from anyone who had its bundle ID. An anonymous caller now gets HTTP 403 for a sync bundle. `POST /drop/file/:bundleId` and `POST /drop/chunk/:bundleId` answer HTTP 404 for an existing sync bundle that has neither an owner nor a stash. A sync bundle that has an owner or belongs to a stash is not affected.

items.title: Send whole numbers and valid addresses to the bundle init routes
items.body: A client that calls `/drop/init` or `/stash/:slug/init` must send `fileCount` and `skippedCount` as whole numbers, `skippedFiles` as a list of `{ path, reason }`, and only valid addresses in `allowedEmails`. Other values are refused with HTTP 400. The upload page that this release serves sends these fields in that form.

items.title: Retry a password request refused with 503
items.body: A script that signs in, unlocks a share link or creates a password-protected bundle can receive HTTP 503 with a `Retry-After` header while other password checks are queued. Wait for the given number of seconds and send the request again.

items.title: Update SIEM rules that match CADF placeholder IDs
items.body: A rule that matched the CADF initiator ID `unknown` or the target ID `n/a` in an audit export needs `blamejs:unattributed` or `blamejs:unidentified` instead.

items.title: Update log queries that use renamed fields
items.body: Some log fields are renamed. `Bundle unlock lockout` and `Zip skip` name the bundle with `bundleId`, and `[files/download] Error` and `[migration] Failed to migrate file` name the file with `fileId`. `[Sync] WebSocket connected` has `bundleId`, `userId` and `since` fields in place of `bundleId`, `user` and `url`. `requireAdmin denied` has `userId` and `role` in place of `user`. `Chunk save failed` no longer has a `bundle` field. `[expiry-cleanup] Failed to remove chunk directory for stale bundle` no longer has `bundleShareId`, and `[orphan-cleanup] Failed to delete empty bundle` no longer has `shareId`. Both keep `bundleId`. The router's `route error` and `middleware error` lines no longer appear. The `Unhandled server error` line reports a server error, and the debug-level `Request refused` line reports a request refused with a 4xx status.

items.title: Replace a `BACKUP_PASSPHRASE_HASH` the server cannot check
items.body: If a backup run or restore fails with "BACKUP_PASSPHRASE_HASH cannot be checked", set `BACKUP_PASSPHRASE_HASH` to an Argon2id hash of the backup passphrase generated at m=65536, t=3, p=4. Its PHC string starts with `$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$`.
